verses.text: King David was very old. No matter how many covers they put on him, he couldn't get warm.
His servants told him, “Let us find a young virgin for my lord the king. She can attend to you and care for you. She can lie close to you so my lord the king can keep warm.”
They searched all over Israel for a beautiful young woman. They found Abishag from Shunem and brought her to the king.
She was very beautiful. She cared for the king and served him, and the king never slept with her.
Then Adonijah son of Haggith put himself forward and said, “I'll be king.” He got chariots and horsemen for himself, with fifty men to run ahead of him.
His father had never once challenged him by asking, “Why did you do that?” Adonijah was also very handsome, and he had been born after Absalom.
He consulted Joab son of Zeruiah and Abiathar the priest, and they backed Adonijah and helped him.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David's elite warriors stayed out of it.
Adonijah slaughtered sheep, cattle, and fattened animals by the stone of Zoheleth near En Rogel. He invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the royal servants from Judah.
He left out Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the elite warriors, and his brother Solomon.
Nathan asked Solomon's mother Bathsheba, “Haven't you heard that Adonijah son of Haggith is ruling as king, and our lord David doesn't even know?
Please take my advice so you can save your life and the life of your son Solomon.
Go to King David and ask him, ‘My lord the king, didn't you swear to me, “Your son Solomon will reign after me and sit on my throne”? Then why is Adonijah ruling?’
While you're still talking to the king, I'll come in after you and confirm what you've said.”
Bathsheba went into the king's room. The king was very old, and Abishag from Shunem was attending him.
Bathsheba bowed respectfully to the king. “What do you want?” he asked.
She said, “My lord, you swore to me by the LORD your God, ‘Your son Solomon will reign after me and sit on my throne.’
And now Adonijah is ruling, and you, my lord the king, don't even know it.
He's slaughtered plenty of cattle, fattened animals, and sheep. He's invited all your sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the army commander. But he didn't invite your servant Solomon.
My lord the king, all Israel is watching you, waiting for you to tell them who will sit on your throne after you.
If you say nothing, then when my lord the king rests with his ancestors, my son Solomon and I will be treated as criminals.”
While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet arrived.
The king was told, “Nathan the prophet is here.” Nathan came in and bowed to the king with his face to the ground.
Nathan asked, “My lord the king, did you say, ‘Adonijah will reign after me and sit on my throne’?

He went down today and slaughtered plenty of cattle, fattened animals, and sheep. He invited all the king's sons, the army commanders, and Abiathar the priest. They're eating and drinking with him and shouting, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’
But he didn't invite me, your servant, or Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon.
Did you order this, my lord the king, without telling your servants who would sit on your throne after you?”
King David answered, “Call Bathsheba back in.” She came and stood before the king.
The king gave his oath: “As surely as the LORD lives, who rescued me from every trouble,
I'll do today exactly what I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel. Your son Solomon will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne in my place.”
Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground in respect and said, “May my lord King David live forever!”
King David said, “Send for Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada.” They came before the king.
He told them, “Take my servants with you. Put my son Solomon on my own mule and take him down to Gihon.
Have Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him king over Israel there. Blow the trumpet and shout, ‘Long live King Solomon!’
Then follow him back up. He'll come and sit on my throne, because he'll be king in my place. I've appointed him to rule Israel and Judah.”
Benaiah son of Jehoiada answered, “Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, declare it so.
Just as the LORD has been with my lord the king, may he be with Solomon and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David.”
Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and Pelethites went down, put Solomon on King David's mule, and brought him to Gihon.
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the Tent and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the trumpet and everyone shouted, “Long live King Solomon!”
All the people followed Solomon back up, playing pipes and celebrating so loudly that the ground shook with the sound.
Adonijah and all his guests heard it as they finished eating. When Joab heard the trumpet, he asked, “Why is the city in such an uproar?”
While he was speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said, “Come in. You're a man of standing, so you must be bringing good news.”
Jonathan answered Adonijah, “Our lord King David has indeed made Solomon king.
The king sent Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and Pelethites with him, and they put him on the king's mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed him king at Gihon. They came back from there celebrating, and the whole city rang with the sound. That's the noise you're hearing.
Solomon is already sitting on the royal throne.
The king's servants went in to bless our lord King David. They said, ‘May your God make Solomon's name greater than yours and make his throne greater than yours.’ Then the king bowed in his bed.
And the king said, ‘Praise the LORD, the God of Israel! He's given me someone to sit on my throne today and let me see it with my own eyes.’”
All Adonijah's guests were terrified. They got up and went their separate ways.
Adonijah was afraid of Solomon. He got up, went to the altar, and grabbed its horns.

Someone told Solomon, “Adonijah is afraid of King Solomon. He's holding on to the horns of the altar and saying, ‘Let King Solomon swear to me first that he won't put his servant to death with the sword.’”
Solomon said, “If he proves himself trustworthy, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground. But if he's found doing wrong, he'll die.”
King Solomon sent men to bring him down from the altar. Adonijah came and bowed before King Solomon, and Solomon told him, “Go home.”
As David's death drew near, he gave his son Solomon these instructions:
“I'm going the way everyone on earth goes. Be strong and show yourself a man.

Follow the instructions of the LORD your God. Walk in his ways and keep his statutes, commands, rulings, and testimonies as written in the law of Moses. Then you'll succeed in all you do and wherever you go.

The LORD will keep the promise he made about me: ‘If your descendants watch how they live and walk faithfully before me with all their heart and soul, there will always be one of your family on the throne of Israel.’

“You also know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me and what he did to the two commanders of Israel's armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He killed them in peacetime as if it were war, staining his belt and sandals with blood.
Act according to your wisdom, and don't let him go down to the grave in peace in his old age.
But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai from Gilead. Give them a place at your table, because their family came to my aid when I ran from your brother Absalom.

“You also have Shimei son of Gera, the Benjamite from Bahurim. He cursed me bitterly the day I went to Mahanaim. But he came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by the LORD, ‘I won't put you to death by the sword.’
Don't treat him as innocent. You're wise and will know what to do with him. Bring his gray head down to the grave in blood.”
David died and joined his ancestors, and he was buried in David's City.
David ruled over Israel for forty years. He ruled seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
Solomon took the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established.
Then Adonijah son of Haggith came to Solomon's mother Bathsheba. “Do you come in peace?” she asked. “In peace,” he answered.
He added, “I have something to tell you.” She said, “Go ahead.”
He said, “You know the kingdom was mine and all Israel expected me to rule. But everything turned around. The kingdom went to my brother because the LORD gave it to him.
Now I have one thing to ask. Please don't turn me down.” She said, “Go ahead.”
He said, “Please ask King Solomon to give me Abishag from Shunem as my wife. He won't say no to you.”
Bathsheba answered, “All right. I'll speak to the king for you.”

Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak for Adonijah. The king got up to meet her and bowed to her. Then he sat on his throne and had another throne set out for his mother, and she sat at his right hand.
She said, “I have one small favor to ask. Please don't turn me down.” The king said, “Ask, Mother. I won't turn you down.”
She answered, “Let Abishag from Shunem be given to your brother Adonijah as his wife.”

King Solomon told his mother, “Why ask for Abishag from Shunem for Adonijah? You might as well ask for the kingdom for him too. He's my older brother, and Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah are with him.”
King Solomon swore by the LORD, “May God punish me severely if Adonijah doesn't pay for this request with his life!
As surely as the LORD lives, who established me and put me on my father David's throne and gave me a royal family as he promised, Adonijah will be put to death today.”
King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who struck Adonijah down and killed him.

The king told Abiathar the priest, “Go back to your fields at Anathoth. You deserve to die, but I won't put you to death today. You carried the ark of the Lord GOD before my father David and shared in all my father's suffering.”
So Solomon removed Abiathar from his service as a priest of the LORD. This fulfilled what the LORD had said at Shiloh about Eli's family.
When the news reached Joab, he ran to the LORD's Tent and clung to the horns of the altar. Joab had backed Adonijah, although he hadn't backed Absalom.
King Solomon heard that Joab had fled to the LORD's Tent and was beside the altar. Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada and told him, “Go strike him down.”
Benaiah came to the LORD's Tent and told Joab, “The king says to come out.” Joab answered, “No. I'll die here.” Benaiah went back to the king and reported exactly what Joab had said.
The king told Benaiah, “Do what he said. Strike him down and bury him. That way you'll remove from me and my father's family the guilt for the blood Joab shed without cause.

The LORD will hold him responsible for the blood he spilled. He attacked and killed two men who were better and more upright than he was, without my father David knowing. They were Abner son of Ner, Israel's army commander, and Amasa son of Jether, Judah's army commander.
Responsibility for their blood will fall on Joab and his descendants forever. But David, his descendants, his family, and his throne will have peace from the LORD forever.”
So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, struck Joab down, and killed him. Joab was buried at his own home in the wilderness.
The king put Benaiah son of Jehoiada in command of the army in Joab's place, and he put Zadok the priest in Abiathar's place.
The king sent for Shimei and told him, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there. Don't leave for anywhere else.
The day you go out and cross the Kidron stream, you can be sure you'll die. Your blood will be on your own head.”
Shimei said to the king, “That's fair. I'll do what my lord the king has said.” So Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.
Three years later, two of Shimei's slaves ran away to Achish son of Maacah, the king of Gath. Someone told Shimei, “Your slaves are in Gath.”
Shimei got up, saddled his donkey, and went to Achish at Gath to look for his slaves. He found them and brought them back from Gath.
Solomon heard that Shimei had left Jerusalem for Gath and returned.
The king sent for Shimei and asked him, “Didn't I make you swear by the LORD and warn you, ‘The day you go anywhere else, you can be sure you'll die’? And you told me, ‘What you've said is fair.’
Why didn't you keep your oath to the LORD and obey what I commanded you?”
The king went on, “Shimei, you know in your own heart all the wrong you did to my father David. The LORD will bring that wrong back on your own head.
But King Solomon will be blessed, and David's throne will stand secure before the LORD forever.”
Then the king gave the order to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who went out and struck Shimei down. So the kingdom was firmly in Solomon's hands.
Solomon made an alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt by marrying his daughter. He brought her to David's City until he finished building his palace, the LORD's house, and the wall around Jerusalem.
The people were still offering sacrifices at the high places because a house hadn't yet been built for the LORD's name.
Solomon loved the LORD and followed the instructions of his father David, though he still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice because it was the main high place. He offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar there.
That night at Gibeon, the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream. God said, “Ask me for what you want me to give you.”

Solomon replied, “You've shown great faithful love to my father David, your servant, because he lived before you faithfully and did what was right with an honest heart. You've kept showing him that love by giving him a son to sit on his throne today.
Now, LORD my God, you've made me king in place of my father David. I'm still like a little child, and I don't know how to lead.
Here I am among the people you've chosen, a nation so large nobody can count them.
So give me an understanding heart to judge your people and tell right from wrong. Who can judge this great people of yours without it?”
The Lord was pleased that Solomon had asked for this.
God said to him, “You asked for understanding so you could judge fairly. You didn't ask for a long life or wealth for yourself, or for the death of your enemies.
So I'll do what you ask. I've given you a wise and understanding heart. There has never been anyone like you before, and there won't be anyone like you after.
I've also given you wealth and honor, things you didn't ask for. No other king will be like you as long as you live.
And if you follow my ways and keep my statutes and commands as your father David did, I'll give you a long life.”

Solomon woke up and realized it was a dream. He went back to Jerusalem, stood in front of the ark of the LORD's covenant, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and gave a feast for all his servants.
Then two women who worked as prostitutes came and stood before the king.
One of them said, “My lord, this woman and I live in the same house. I gave birth while she was there.
She had her baby three days after I had mine. We were alone together. There was nobody else in the house.
Her baby died in the night because she lay on top of him.
She got up in the middle of the night while I was asleep and took my son from beside me. She laid him against her chest and laid her dead baby against mine.
When I got up in the morning to nurse my son, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning light, I saw he wasn't the son I'd given birth to.”

The other woman said, “No! The living baby is my son, and the dead one is yours.” The first woman answered, “No! The dead baby is yours, and the living baby is mine.” They argued back and forth in front of the king.
The king said, “One of you says, ‘My son is the one who's alive, and yours is the one who died.’ The other says, ‘No, yours is dead, and mine is alive.’”
Then he said, “Bring me a sword.” They brought one to him.
The king ordered, “Cut the living child in two. Give each woman half.”

The woman whose child was alive was overcome with love for her son. She pleaded with the king, “Please, my lord, give her the living baby. Just don't kill him!” The other said, “He won't be mine or yours. Cut him in two.”
The king answered, “Give the first woman the living child. Don't harm him. She's his mother.”
All Israel heard how the king had ruled. They stood in awe of him because they saw that God had given him the wisdom to judge justly.
King Solomon ruled over all Israel.
These were his senior officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest.
Elihoreph and Ahijah, sons of Shisha, were the scribes, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the official records.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the army. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the officers. Zabud son of Nathan was the chief minister and the king's friend.
Ahishar ran the palace household, and Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of forced labor.
Solomon appointed twelve officers across Israel to supply food for the king and his household. Each was responsible for one month of the year.
These were their names and districts: Ben Hur served in the hill country of Ephraim.
Ben Deker served in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth Shemesh, and Elon Beth Hanan.
Ben Hesed served in Arubboth, including Socoh and all the land of Hepher.
Ben Abinadab served in the whole highland of Dor. He was married to Solomon's daughter Taphath.
Baana son of Ahilud served in Taanach, Megiddo, and all of Beth Shean near Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth Shean to Abel Meholah and beyond Jokmeam.
Ben Geber served in Ramoth Gilead. His district included the towns of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead and the region of Argob in Bashan, with sixty large cities that had walls and bronze gate bars.
Ahinadab son of Iddo served in Mahanaim.
Ahimaaz served in Naphtali. He married Solomon's daughter Basemath.
Baana son of Hushai served in Asher and Bealoth.
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah served in Issachar.
Shimei son of Ela served in Benjamin.
Geber son of Uri served in Gilead, the former territory of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. He was the only officer in that land.
The people of Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand by the sea. They ate, drank, and enjoyed themselves.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and on to Egypt's border. They paid him tribute and served him as long as he lived.
Solomon's household needed thirty cors of fine flour and sixty measures of meal every day,
along with ten fattened cattle, twenty cattle from the pasture, a hundred sheep, and deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened birds.
Solomon ruled over all the land west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, and over all the kings in that region. There was peace on every side.
Judah and Israel lived in safety from Dan to Beersheba throughout Solomon's reign. Everyone could sit under their own vine and fig tree.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls for his chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen.
Each officer supplied food for King Solomon and everyone who ate at his table during the month he was responsible for. They made sure nothing ran short.
They also brought barley and straw for the horses and swift steeds wherever they were needed, each officer doing his part.
God gave Solomon abundant wisdom, deep understanding, and a mind as wide-ranging as the sand on the seashore is plentiful.
Solomon's wisdom surpassed that of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than anyone else, including Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. His fame spread through all the nations around him.
He spoke three thousand proverbs and composed a thousand and five songs.
He spoke about plants, from the cedars of Lebanon to the hyssop growing out of a wall. He also spoke about animals, birds, creatures that crawl, and fish.
People from every nation came to hear Solomon's wisdom. Kings across the earth heard about it and sent them to listen.
Hiram king of Tyre heard that Solomon had been anointed to take his father's place as king. Hiram had always loved David, so he sent his servants to Solomon.
Solomon sent this message back to Hiram:
“You know my father David couldn't build a house for the name of the LORD his God. He faced wars on every side until the LORD put his enemies under his feet.
But now the LORD my God has given me peace all around. I have no enemy to face and no disaster to contend with.
I plan to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, just as the LORD said to my father David: ‘Your son, whom I'll put on your throne in your place, will build the house for my name.’

Please give orders to cut down cedars from Lebanon for me. My workers will join yours, and I'll pay whatever wages you set for your workers. You know that nobody among us can cut timber the way the Sidonians can.”
When Hiram heard Solomon's message, he was overjoyed. “Praise the LORD today,” he said, “for giving David a wise son to rule this great people.”
Hiram sent word to Solomon: “I've heard your message. I'll supply all the cedar and cypress timber you want.

My workers will bring the logs down from Lebanon to the sea. I'll have them tied into rafts and floated to whatever place you name. I'll have them taken apart there for you to pick up. In return, I'd like you to supply food for my household.”
So Hiram supplied Solomon with as much cedar and cypress timber as he wanted.
Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat to feed his household and twenty cors of pure olive oil. He gave Hiram this amount every year.
The LORD gave Solomon wisdom as he had promised. Hiram and Solomon were at peace and made a treaty with each other.
King Solomon drafted workers from all over Israel for forced labor. The work force numbered thirty thousand men.
He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand a month. They spent one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon had seventy thousand men carrying loads and eighty thousand cutting stone in the mountains.
He also had thirty-three hundred supervisors in charge of the people doing the work.
At the king's command they quarried large, costly stones and dressed them for the foundation of the house.
Solomon's builders, Hiram's builders, and the men of Gebal cut the materials and prepared the timber and stone to build the house.
In the four hundred and eightieth year after Israel left Egypt, Solomon began building the LORD's house. It was the fourth year of his reign over Israel, in Ziv, the second month.
The house King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
The porch at the front ran twenty cubits across the width of the building and extended ten cubits out from it.
Solomon made windows with fixed latticework for the house.
He built a structure with several floors against the walls all around the temple hall and inner sanctuary. He made rooms along the sides of the building.

The rooms on the lowest floor were five cubits wide, the middle ones six cubits wide, and the top ones seven cubits wide. He made ledges on the outside of the temple wall to support the beams without cutting into the walls.
The stone was cut at the quarry before it reached the building site. No hammer, ax, or other iron tool could be heard in the house while it was being built.
The entrance to the middle side rooms was on the right side of the house. Winding stairs led up to the middle floor and from there to the third.
Solomon built and finished the house, roofing it with cedar beams and planks.
He built the stories along the whole house, each five cubits high, and attached them to the house with cedar timbers.
The LORD gave Solomon this message:
“About this house you're building, if you follow my statutes, carry out my rulings, and keep all my commands, I'll keep the promise I made to your father David through you.
I'll live among the Israelites and never abandon my people Israel.”
So Solomon finished building the house.
He lined the inside walls with cedar boards from floor to ceiling and laid cypress boards on the floor.
At the back of the house he used cedar boards from floor to ceiling to build a room twenty cubits deep. He made it the inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place.
The temple hall in front of the inner sanctuary was forty cubits long.
The cedar inside was carved with buds and open flowers. Cedar covered everything, so no stone could be seen.
Solomon prepared the inner sanctuary inside the house to hold the ark of the LORD's covenant.
The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. He covered it with pure gold and covered the altar with cedar.
Solomon covered the inside of the house with pure gold. He stretched gold chains across the front of the inner sanctuary and covered it with gold.
He continued until the whole house was covered in gold. He also covered the entire altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary with gold.
He made two cherubim out of olive wood for the inner sanctuary. Each stood ten cubits high.
Each wing of the first cherub measured five cubits. It was ten cubits across from one wingtip to the other.
The other cherub also measured ten cubits. Both cherubim had the same size and shape.
Each cherub stood ten cubits high.

He placed the cherubim inside the inner sanctuary with their wings stretched out. One touched the wall on one side, and the other touched the opposite wall. Their other wings met in the middle of the room.
He covered both cherubim with gold.
All around the walls of the house, in the inner and outer rooms, he carved cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers.
He covered the floor with gold in both the inner and outer rooms.
For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made olive-wood doors. The lintel and doorposts took up a fifth of the wall.
He carved cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers into the two olive-wood doors and covered them with gold, pressing the gold onto the carved cherubim and palm trees.
He also made olive-wood doorposts for the entrance to the temple hall. They took up a fourth of the wall.
He made two cypress doors, each with two folding panels.
He carved cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers into the doors and fitted gold over the carvings.
He built the inner courtyard with three rows of cut stone and one row of cedar beams.
The builders laid the foundation of the LORD's house in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv.
In the eleventh year, in Bul, the eighth month, every part of the house was finished according to its plans. It took Solomon seven years to build it.
Solomon spent thirteen years building his palace before the whole complex was finished.
He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. It was a hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. Four rows of cedar pillars held up cedar beams.
Cedar roofing covered forty-five beams that rested on the pillars, fifteen to a row.
There were three rows of beams, with windows facing each other in three tiers.
All the doors and doorposts had square frames made of beams, and the windows faced each other in three tiers.
He built the Hall of Pillars, fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. It had a porch in front, with pillars and a threshold.
He built the throne hall where he would hear cases, the Hall of Judgment, and lined it with cedar from floor to floor.
His own living quarters were in another courtyard behind the hall and were built the same way. He also built a house like the hall for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he'd married.
All these buildings were made of costly stone, cut to size and sawed on both faces. This was true from the foundations to the coping and out as far as the main courtyard.
The foundations used large, costly stones, some ten cubits long and others eight cubits long.
Above them were costly stones cut to size and cedar timber.
The main courtyard was surrounded by three rows of cut stone and one row of cedar beams, just like the inner courtyard of the LORD's house and its porch.
King Solomon sent for Hiram from Tyre.

His mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a bronze worker from Tyre. Hiram had the knowledge, insight, and skill to do any kind of bronze work. He came to King Solomon and did all the work assigned to him.
He made two bronze pillars, each eighteen cubits high and twelve cubits around.
He cast two bronze capitals to go on top of the pillars. Each capital was five cubits high.
The capitals on the pillars had latticework and chain wreaths, seven on each capital.
He finished the pillars with two rows of pomegranates around the latticework that covered each capital. He decorated both capitals the same way.
The capitals at the top of the porch pillars were shaped like lilies and measured four cubits.
The capitals on the two pillars rose above the rounded part beside the lattice. Two hundred pomegranates stood in rows around the other capital.
Hiram set up the pillars at the temple porch. He named the right pillar Jachin and the left pillar Boaz.
The tops of the pillars were decorated with lily designs. That completed the work on the pillars.
Hiram cast a round basin called the Sea. It measured ten cubits across the rim, five cubits high, and thirty cubits around.
Two rows of buds ran around the Sea below its rim, with ten to a cubit. The buds were cast in one piece with the basin.
The Sea stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three west, three south, and three east. The basin rested on their backs, and the hindquarters of all twelve faced inward.
The basin was a handbreadth thick. The rim curved like the rim of a cup, shaped like a lily blossom. It held two thousand baths.
Hiram made ten bronze stands. Each was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.
The stands were built in framed sections, with panels between the rails.
Lions, oxen, and cherubim decorated the panels between the rails. There was a pedestal above the rails and hanging wreaths below the lions and oxen.
Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles, and supports at its four corners. The supports were cast beneath the basin, with wreaths beside them.
The opening extended one cubit inside the crown and above it. It was round like a pedestal, measuring a cubit and a half. There were engraved designs around the opening, and the panels were square.
The four wheels sat below the panels, with their axles mounted in the stand. Each wheel was a cubit and a half high.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels. The axles, rims, spokes, and hubs were all cast metal.
There were four supports, one at each corner, cast as part of the stand itself.
At the top of each stand was a round band half a cubit high. Its supports and panels were part of the same piece.
Hiram engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees on the support plates and panels wherever there was space, with wreaths all around.
He made all ten stands the same way, each with the same casting, size, and shape.
He made ten bronze basins. Each basin measured four cubits and held forty baths. A basin sat on each of the ten stands.
He set five stands on the right side of the house and five on the left. He put the Sea on the right side of the house, toward the southeast.
Hiram made the pots, shovels, and basins. Here's everything he finished for King Solomon in the LORD's house:
the two pillars, the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of them, and the two pieces of latticework that covered the capitals;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two pieces of latticework, in two rows on each piece to cover the bowl-shaped capitals on the pillars;
the ten stands and the ten basins that sat on them;
the Sea and the twelve oxen beneath it;
and the pots, shovels, and basins. All the furnishings Hiram made for King Solomon for the LORD's house were polished bronze.
The king had them cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan.
Solomon didn't weigh the furnishings because there were so many. Nobody determined the bronze's total weight.
Solomon made all the furnishings for the LORD's house, including the gold altar and the gold table for the bread of the Presence.
He made five lampstands for the right side and five for the left in front of the inner sanctuary, all of pure gold. He made their flowers, lamps, and tongs out of gold.
He made the cups, wick trimmers, basins, spoons, and firepans of pure gold. He also made gold hinges for the doors of the Most Holy Place and for the doors of the temple hall.
When King Solomon finished all the work on the LORD's house, he brought in the silver, gold, and vessels his father David had dedicated and put them in the treasuries of the LORD's house.
Solomon called Israel's elders, the heads of its tribes, and the leaders of its families to Jerusalem. They were to bring the ark of the LORD's covenant up from David's City, also called Zion.
All the men of Israel gathered before King Solomon for the festival in Ethanim, the seventh month.
Once Israel's elders had arrived, the priests lifted the ark.
The priests and Levites carried up the LORD's ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the sacred furnishings that were in the Tent.
King Solomon and all the Israelites who had gathered with him stood before the ark. They sacrificed more sheep and cattle than anyone could count.
The priests brought the ark of the LORD's covenant into its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim.
The cherubim spread their wings over the ark, covering the ark and its carrying poles from above.
The poles were so long that their ends could be seen from the Holy Place in front of the inner sanctuary. They couldn't be seen from outside, and they're still there today.
The only things in the ark were the two stone tablets Moses had put there at Horeb when the LORD made a covenant with Israel after they came out of Egypt.
When the priests came out of the Holy Place, the cloud filled the LORD's house.
The priests couldn't stand there to serve because of the cloud. The LORD's glory filled his house.
Solomon said, “The LORD said he would live in thick darkness.
I've built you a home, a place for you to live forever.”
The king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel while they stood.
He said, “Praise the LORD, the God of Israel! He gave your father David his word, and with his own hand he's kept it. He said,
‘Since I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I haven't chosen a city in any tribe to build a house for my name. I chose David to lead my people Israel.’
“My father David wanted to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
But the LORD told my father David, ‘You did well to want to build a house for my name.
Still, you won't build the house. Your own son will build the house for my name.’
The LORD has kept his promise. I've taken my father's place and sit on Israel's throne, just as the LORD said. I've built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
I've made a place there for the ark, which holds the covenant the LORD made with our ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt.”
Solomon stood in front of the LORD's altar with all Israel gathered there and stretched out his hands toward heaven.
He prayed, “LORD, God of Israel, there's no God like you in heaven above or on earth below. You keep your covenant and show faithful love to your servants who walk before you with their whole heart.
You've kept the promise you made to your servant David, my father. You said it with your own mouth and carried it out with your own hand, as we can see today.

Now, LORD, God of Israel, keep your promise to my father David, your servant: ‘You will always have someone before me on Israel's throne, as long as your descendants watch their steps and walk before me as you have.’
Now, God of Israel, please let the word you spoke to your servant David, my father, come true.
But will God really live on earth? The heavens, even the highest heavens, can't hold you. How could this house I built ever hold you?
Still, LORD my God, pay attention to your servant's prayer and plea. Hear the cry and the prayer I'm bringing before you today.
Keep your eyes on this house night and day, on the place where you said, ‘My name will be there.’ Hear your servant's prayer when I turn toward this place.
Hear your servant and your people Israel when we pray toward this place. Listen from heaven, where you live, and when you hear us, forgive us.
“If someone wrongs a neighbor and is required to take an oath, and comes to swear before your altar in this house,

hear from heaven and act. Judge between your servants. Condemn the guilty and bring the consequences of what they've done on their own head. Clear the innocent and give them what their upright conduct deserves.
“When your people Israel are defeated by an enemy because they have sinned against you, if they come back to you, acknowledge your name, and pray and plead with you in this house,
hear from heaven. Forgive your people Israel and bring them back to the land you gave their ancestors.
“When the sky closes and rain stops because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place, acknowledge your name, and turn from their sin because you've afflicted them,
hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel. Teach them the good way they should live and send rain to the land you gave them as their inheritance.
“If there's famine, plague, blight, mildew, locusts, or caterpillars, or if an enemy lays siege to their cities, whatever disease or disaster comes,
and someone, or all your people Israel, prays for help, each knowing the pain within their own heart and stretching out their hands toward this house,
hear from heaven where you live. Forgive them and act. Give each person what their conduct deserves, because you know their hearts. You alone know every human heart.
Then they'll honor you all the days they live in the land you gave our ancestors.
“When a foreigner who doesn't belong to your people Israel comes from a distant land because of your name,
because people will hear about your great name, your mighty hand, and your outstretched arm, and that foreigner prays toward this house,

hear from heaven where you live and do all that the foreigner asks of you. Then all the peoples of the earth will know your name and honor you as your people Israel do. They'll know that this house I built bears your name.
“When your people go out to fight their enemies wherever you send them, if they pray to the LORD toward the city you've chosen and the house I've built for your name,
hear their prayer and their plea from heaven and uphold their cause.
“If they sin against you, and everyone sins, and you become angry and hand them over to an enemy who takes them captive to a land far away or nearby,
but they come to their senses there and turn back and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, ‘We've sinned, we've done wrong, and we've acted wickedly,’

if they turn back to you with their whole heart and soul in the land of their enemies, and pray toward the land you gave their ancestors, the city you've chosen, and the house I've built for your name,
hear their prayer and their plea from heaven where you live, and uphold their cause.
Forgive your people for sinning against you and for all the ways they've rebelled against you. Move their captors to show them compassion,
because they are your people and your inheritance, whom you brought out of Egypt, out of the middle of the iron furnace.
Keep your eyes open to your servant's plea and to the pleas of your people Israel, and hear them whenever they call out to you.
You set them apart from all the peoples of the earth as your own inheritance, just as you said through your servant Moses when you brought our ancestors out of Egypt, Lord GOD.”
When Solomon finished his prayer and plea to the LORD, he got up from his knees in front of the LORD's altar, where he'd been kneeling with his hands spread toward heaven.
He stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel in a loud voice:
“Praise the LORD, who has given his people Israel rest, just as he promised. Every word of the good promise he gave through his servant Moses has come true.
May the LORD our God be with us as he was with our ancestors. May he never leave us or turn away from us.
May he turn our hearts toward him so we'll walk in all his ways and keep the commands, statutes, and rulings he gave our ancestors.
May the words I've prayed before the LORD stay close to the LORD our God day and night. May he uphold my cause and the cause of his people Israel as each day requires.
Then all the peoples of the earth will know that the LORD himself is God. There is no other.
Give your whole heart to the LORD our God so you follow his statutes and keep his commands, as you're doing today.”
Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifices before the LORD.
Solomon offered twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep as peace offerings to the LORD. The king and all Israel dedicated the LORD's house this way.

That same day the king set apart the middle of the courtyard in front of the LORD's house as holy. He offered the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings there because the bronze altar before the LORD was too small for them all.

So Solomon and all Israel kept the festival before the LORD our God. A great crowd came from the entrance to Hamath all the way to the Brook of Egypt. They celebrated for seven days and then seven more, fourteen days altogether.
On the eighth day he sent the people home. They blessed the king and went back to their tents full of joy for all the good the LORD had done for his servant David and for his people Israel.
Solomon finished the LORD's house, his own palace, and everything else he'd wanted to build.
The LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, just as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.
The LORD told him, “I've heard the prayer and plea you brought before me. I've set apart this house you built as holy and put my name here forever. My eyes and my heart will always be here.
As for you, walk before me just as your father David did, with an honest and upright heart. Do everything I've commanded you and keep my statutes and rulings.
Then I'll establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised your father David when I said, ‘There will always be a man from your family on Israel's throne.’
But if you or your descendants turn away from me, disregard the commands and statutes I've given you, and go serve and worship other gods,
I'll cut Israel off from the land I've given them. I'll cast this house I've made holy for my name out of my sight, and people everywhere will use Israel's name as a saying and an insult.
This house stands high now, but everyone who passes by it will be shocked and hiss. They'll ask, ‘Why has the LORD done this to this land and this house?’

People will answer, ‘Because they abandoned the LORD their God, who brought their ancestors out of Egypt. They embraced other gods and worshiped and served them. That's why the LORD brought all this disaster on them.’”
Solomon spent twenty years building the two houses, the LORD's house and the royal palace.
Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with all the cedar, cypress, and gold he wanted. At the end of those years, King Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in Galilee.
Hiram came from Tyre to see the towns Solomon had given him, and he wasn't pleased with them.
“What kind of towns have you given me, my brother?” he asked. He called them the land of Cabul, as they're still called today.
Hiram sent the king a hundred and twenty talents of gold.
King Solomon drafted workers for forced labor to build the LORD's house, his palace, the Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, and the towns of Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.
Pharaoh king of Egypt had captured Gezer, burned it, and killed the Canaanites who lived there. He gave the town as a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon's wife.
Solomon rebuilt Gezer and Lower Beth Horon,
as well as Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness,
all his storage towns, the towns for his chariots and horsemen, and whatever else he chose to build in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and the rest of his kingdom.
Some Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites still lived in the land. They weren't Israelites.
The Israelites hadn't been able to wipe out their descendants. Solomon conscripted them for forced labor, and that service continues to this day.
Solomon made none of the Israelites serve as forced laborers. They were his soldiers, servants, officials, captains, and commanders of his chariots and horsemen.
Solomon had five hundred and fifty chief officers who supervised the people doing the work.
Pharaoh's daughter moved up from David's City to the palace Solomon had built for her. Then Solomon built the Millo.
Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he had built for the LORD. He also burned incense before the LORD. So he completed the house.
King Solomon built a fleet at Ezion Geber near Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea in Edom.
Hiram sent his own experienced sailors to serve in the fleet with Solomon's men.
They sailed to Ophir, took on four hundred and twenty talents of gold, and brought it back to King Solomon.
When the queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's fame in connection with the LORD's name, she came to test him with hard questions.
She arrived in Jerusalem with a huge caravan of camels carrying spices, a great deal of gold, and precious stones. When she met Solomon, she talked with him about everything on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions. There was nothing she asked that the king couldn't explain.
The queen of Sheba saw Solomon's wisdom and the palace he had built.
She saw the food on his table, the seating of his servants, how his officials attended him, their clothes, his cupbearers, and the way he went up to the LORD's house. It took her breath away.
She told the king, “The report I heard at home about your deeds and your wisdom was true.
I didn't believe it until I came and saw it myself. I'd been told less than half of it! Your wisdom and prosperity go beyond what I heard.
How fortunate your people are! How fortunate your servants are to stand before you every day and hear your wisdom!
Praise the LORD your God, who delighted in you and put you on Israel's throne. Because the LORD loves Israel forever, he made you king to do what is just and right.”
She gave King Solomon a hundred and twenty talents of gold, a huge amount of spices, and precious stones. No one ever brought him as many spices again as the queen of Sheba did.
Hiram's fleet, which brought gold from Ophir, also brought large quantities of almug wood and precious stones from there.

The king used the almug wood to make pillars for the LORD's house and the palace, and harps and other stringed instruments for the singers. Nothing like that almug wood has arrived or been seen since.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she asked for, as well as the generous gifts he chose to give her as king. Then she and her servants went back to her own country.
Solomon received six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold in a year,
besides what came from traders, merchants, the kings of the various peoples, and the governors of the land.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold, using six hundred shekels of gold for each one.
He also made three hundred smaller shields of hammered gold, using three minas of gold for each. The king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king made a great ivory throne and covered it with the finest gold.
Six steps led up to the throne, which had a rounded top at the back. The seat had an armrest on either side, with a lion standing beside each armrest.
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one on each side of every step. No other kingdom had made anything like it.
All King Solomon's drinking cups were gold, and all the vessels in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. None were silver, because silver was considered worth little in Solomon's time.
The king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with Hiram's fleet. Once every three years his fleet came back with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon surpassed every other king on earth in wealth and wisdom.
People from all over the earth sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart.
Year after year each visitor brought a gift: silver and gold vessels, clothes, armor, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen until he had fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed them in the chariot towns and kept some with him in Jerusalem.
The king made silver as common as stones in Jerusalem and cedar as common as sycamore trees in the lowlands.
Solomon's horses came from Egypt. The king's merchants bought them in herds at an agreed price.
A chariot imported from Egypt cost six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse cost a hundred and fifty. The merchants also exported them to the Hittite and Syrian kings.
King Solomon loved many foreign women besides Pharaoh's daughter. They were Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women.

The LORD had told the Israelites about these nations, “You must not join yourselves to them, and they must not join themselves to you. They'll surely turn your hearts toward their gods.” But Solomon held on to these women in love.
He had seven hundred wives of royal rank and three hundred concubines. His wives turned his heart away.
When Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart toward other gods. His heart wasn't wholly devoted to the LORD his God as his father's heart had been.
Solomon followed Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Milcom, the detestable god of the Ammonites.
Solomon did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He didn't follow the LORD wholeheartedly as his father David had.
On the mountain facing Jerusalem, Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the detestable god of Moab, and for Molech, the detestable god of the Ammonites.
He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and offered sacrifices to their gods.
The LORD was angry with Solomon because his heart had turned from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.
He had commanded Solomon to keep away from other gods, but Solomon disobeyed the LORD's command.
So the LORD told Solomon, “Because you've done this and broken my covenant and the statutes I commanded you to keep, I'll tear the kingdom away from you and give it to one of your servants.
For the sake of your father David, I won't do this during your lifetime. I'll tear it out of your son's hands.
Even then, I won't take the whole kingdom. I'll leave one tribe to your son for the sake of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city I've chosen.”
The LORD raised up an opponent against Solomon named Hadad the Edomite, a descendant of Edom's king.
Back when David was in Edom, Joab the army commander went up to bury the dead and struck down every male in Edom.
Joab and all Israel stayed there for six months, until every male in Edom had been cut down.
Hadad was only a small child at the time. He escaped to Egypt with some Edomites who had served his father.
They left Midian, went to Paran, and took some men from there with them into Egypt. Pharaoh king of Egypt gave Hadad a house, a supply of food, and land.
Pharaoh took such a liking to Hadad that he gave him his own wife's sister in marriage, the sister of Queen Tahpenes.
Tahpenes' sister bore Hadad a son named Genubath. Tahpenes weaned him in Pharaoh's palace, and he lived there among Pharaoh's sons.
When Hadad heard in Egypt that David had died and Joab the army commander was dead too, he told Pharaoh, “Let me leave so I can go home to my own country.”
Pharaoh asked, “What have you lacked here with me that makes you want to go back to your country?” Hadad answered, “Nothing. Please just let me go.”
God raised up another opponent, Rezon son of Eliada. He had fled from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah.
When David killed the men of Zobah, Rezon gathered a band of men and became their leader. They went to Damascus, settled there, and took power in the city.
Alongside the trouble Hadad caused, Rezon opposed Israel throughout Solomon's reign. He despised Israel and ruled over Syria.
Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah and one of Solomon's servants, also rebelled against the king. His mother Zeruah was a widow.
Here's how he came to rebel. Solomon was building the Millo and repairing the breach in the defenses of his father David's City.
Jeroboam was a capable man. When Solomon saw how hard the young man worked, he put him in charge of all the labor from the house of Joseph.
One day Jeroboam left Jerusalem, and Ahijah the prophet from Shiloh met him on the road. Ahijah was wearing a new garment, and the two men were alone in the open country.
Ahijah took off the new garment he was wearing and tore it into twelve pieces.
He told Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces. This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I'm going to tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hands and give ten tribes to you.
He'll keep one tribe for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I've chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.

This is because they've abandoned me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites. They haven't followed my ways, done what's right in my eyes, or kept my statutes and rulings as Solomon's father David did.
“‘I won't take the whole kingdom out of Solomon's hands. I'll let him rule for the rest of his life for the sake of my chosen servant David, who kept my commands and statutes.
I'll take the kingdom from Solomon's son and give ten tribes to you.
I'll give one tribe to his son, so my servant David will always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city I've chosen for my name.
I'll take you and make you king over Israel. You'll rule over all your heart desires.

If you listen to everything I command, follow my ways, do what's right in my eyes, and keep my statutes and commands as my servant David did, I'll be with you. I'll establish a lasting royal family for you as I did for David, and I'll give you Israel.
I'll bring trouble on David's descendants because of this, but it won't last forever.’”
Solomon tried to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam escaped to Shishak king of Egypt and stayed there until Solomon died.
The rest of Solomon's acts, everything he did, and his wisdom are recorded in the Book of the Acts of Solomon.
Solomon ruled over all Israel from Jerusalem for forty years.
Solomon died and joined his ancestors. He was buried in his father David's City, and his son Rehoboam became king in his place.
Rehoboam went to Shechem, where all Israel had gathered to make him king.
Jeroboam son of Nebat heard about it while he was still living in Egypt, where he'd fled from King Solomon.
The people sent for him. Jeroboam and the whole assembly of Israel came to Rehoboam and said,
“Your father put a heavy yoke on us. Lighten the burden he placed on us and the hard labor he demanded, and we'll serve you.”
He told them, “Go away for three days, then come back to me.” So the people left.
King Rehoboam consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon while he was alive. “How do you advise me to answer these people?” he asked.
They replied, “Serve these people today and give them a kind answer. If you take care of them now, they'll serve you always.”
But Rehoboam rejected the elders' advice and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and now served him.
He asked them, “How do you think we should answer these people who told me, ‘Lighten the yoke your father put on us’?”
The young men who had grown up with him replied, “Here's what to tell the people who want you to lighten the heavy yoke your father put on them: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father's waist.
My father put a heavy yoke on you. I'll make it heavier. My father disciplined you with whips, and I'll discipline you with scorpions.’”
Jeroboam and all the people came back to Rehoboam on the third day, just as the king had told them to.
The king answered them harshly. He set aside the advice the elders had given him
and followed the younger men's advice. “My father made your yoke heavy,” he said. “I'll make it heavier. My father disciplined you with whips, and I'll discipline you with scorpions.”
The king refused to listen to the people. The LORD had brought this about to fulfill what he'd told Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah from Shiloh.

When all Israel saw that the king wouldn't listen, they answered, “What share do we have in David? We have no inheritance in Jesse's son. Back to your tents, Israel! Look after your own house now, David.” Then the Israelites went home.
Rehoboam still ruled over the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah.
King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who supervised forced labor, but all Israel stoned him to death. The king scrambled into his chariot and escaped to Jerusalem.
Israel has remained in rebellion against David's house to this day.
When all Israel heard Jeroboam was back, they called him to the assembly and made him king over Israel. Only the tribe of Judah stayed loyal to David's house.
When Rehoboam got to Jerusalem, he gathered Judah and Benjamin, a hundred and eighty thousand chosen warriors, to fight Israel and restore the kingdom to himself, Solomon's son.
But God gave this message to Shemaiah, the man of God:
“Tell Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and all the people of Judah and Benjamin and the rest of the people,
‘This is what the LORD says: Don't go up to fight your fellow Israelites. Everyone go home, because this came from me.’” They listened to the LORD and went home, as he'd told them.
Jeroboam built up Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. From there he went out and built up Penuel.
Jeroboam thought to himself, “The kingdom could go back to David's family now.
If these people go up to offer sacrifices at the LORD's house in Jerusalem, they'll give their loyalty back to their lord, King Rehoboam of Judah. They'll kill me and go back to Rehoboam.”
So the king took advice and made two gold calves. He told the people, “It's too much for you to keep going up to Jerusalem. Here are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt!”
He set one calf in Bethel and the other in Dan.
This led the people into sin. They went as far as Dan to worship before the calf there.
Jeroboam built shrines at the high places and appointed priests from among the people, even though they weren't descendants of Levi.

Jeroboam established a festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the one in Judah. He went up to the altar at Bethel and sacrificed to the calves he'd made. He placed the priests he'd appointed for the high places in Bethel.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a date Jeroboam had picked himself, he went up to the altar he'd built in Bethel. He established a festival for Israel and went to the altar to burn incense.
A man of God came from Judah to Bethel at the LORD's command. Jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense.

At the LORD's command, the man cried out against the altar: “Altar! Altar! This is what the LORD says: ‘A son named Josiah will be born into David's family. On you he'll sacrifice the priests who burn incense on you at the high places, and human bones will be burned on you.’”
That day he gave a sign: “Here's the sign the LORD has announced. This altar will split apart, and its ashes will spill out.”

When Jeroboam heard what the man of God shouted against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar and ordered, “Seize him!” The hand he'd stretched toward the man withered, and he couldn't pull it back.
The altar split apart, and its ashes poured out, just as the man of God had said when he gave the sign from the LORD.

The king told the man of God, “Please ask the LORD your God for mercy and pray for me so my hand will come back to normal.” The man of God pleaded with the LORD, and the king's hand was restored just as it had been before.
The king said to the man of God, “Come home with me and have something to eat. I'll give you a reward.”
The man of God answered, “Even if you gave me half of everything in your house, I wouldn't go with you. I won't eat bread or drink water here,
because the LORD commanded me, ‘Don't eat bread or drink water there, and don't go back the way you came.’”
So he left by a different road and didn't go back the way he'd come into Bethel.
An old prophet lived in Bethel. One of his sons came and told him what the man of God had done there that day. His sons also told their father what the man had said to the king.
Their father asked, “Which way did he go?” His sons had seen which road the man of God from Judah took.
“Saddle my donkey,” he told them. They saddled it, and he rode off.
He went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak tree. “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” he asked. “I am,” the man answered.
The old prophet said to him, “Come home with me and have some bread.”
He replied, “I can't go back with you or go into your house. I won't eat bread or drink water with you here.
The LORD told me, ‘Don't eat bread or drink water there, and don't turn back the way you came.’”
The old prophet said, “I'm a prophet too. An angel gave me this message from the LORD: ‘Bring him back to your house to eat bread and drink water.’” He was lying.
So the man of God went back with him, ate bread in his house, and drank water.
While they were sitting at the table, the LORD gave a message to the prophet who had brought him back.
He called out to the man of God from Judah, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You disobeyed the LORD's word and didn't keep the command the LORD your God gave you.
You came back and ate bread and drank water in the place where he told you, “Don't eat bread or drink water.” So your body won't be buried in your ancestors' tomb.’”
After the man from Judah had eaten and drunk, the old prophet saddled the donkey for the man he'd brought back.
As the man traveled, a lion met him on the road and killed him. His body lay on the road, and the donkey and the lion both stood beside it.
Some people passing by saw the body lying there and the lion standing beside it. They went and told people in the town where the old prophet lived.

When the prophet who had brought him back heard about it, he said, “That's the man of God who disobeyed the LORD's word. So the LORD handed him over to the lion, which mauled and killed him, just as the LORD said would happen.”
He told his sons to saddle the donkey for him, and they did.
He went and found the man's body lying on the road with the donkey and lion standing beside it. The lion hadn't eaten the body or mauled the donkey.
The old prophet lifted the man of God's body onto the donkey and brought it back to his own town to mourn and bury him.
He laid the body in his own grave, and they mourned over him, saying, “Oh, my brother!”
After he buried him, the old prophet told his sons, “When I die, bury me in the tomb where the man of God is buried. Put my bones next to his.
The message he shouted at the LORD's command against the altar in Bethel and all the shrines at the high places in the towns of Samaria will surely come true.”
Even after this, Jeroboam didn't turn from his evil ways. He appointed more priests for the high places from among the people. He consecrated anyone who wanted to be a priest at the high places.
That became a sin for Jeroboam's family and led to its destruction, until it was cut off from the face of the earth.
Around that time Jeroboam's son Abijah fell ill.
Jeroboam told his wife, “Please get up and put on a disguise so nobody recognizes you as my wife. Go to Shiloh. Ahijah the prophet is there, the one who told me I'd become king over these people.
Take ten loaves of bread, some cakes, and a jar of honey. He'll tell you what will happen to the boy.”
Jeroboam's wife did as he asked and went to Ahijah's house in Shiloh. Ahijah had lost his sight in his old age.
But the LORD had told him, “Jeroboam's wife is coming to ask you about her son because he's sick. I'll tell you what to say to her. When she comes in, she'll pretend to be someone else.”
When Ahijah heard her footsteps at the door, he said, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why pretend to be someone else? I've been sent to give you terrible news.
Go tell Jeroboam, ‘This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: “I raised you up from among the people and made you ruler over my people Israel.

I tore the kingdom away from David's family and gave it to you. Yet you haven't lived like my servant David, who kept my commands and followed me with all his heart, doing only what was right in my eyes.
You've done more evil than everyone who came before you. You've made other gods for yourself, cast metal idols, made me angry, and turned your back on me.

So I'll bring disaster on Jeroboam's family. I'll cut off every male of his household in Israel, whether shut in or free. I'll sweep away his family the way someone sweeps away dung until it's all gone.
Dogs will eat anyone from Jeroboam's household who dies in town, and birds will eat anyone who dies out in the fields. The LORD has spoken.”’
Now get up and go home. As soon as you set foot in the city, the boy will die.

All Israel will mourn for him and bury him. He'll be the only one in Jeroboam's family to get a burial, because in that household the LORD, the God of Israel, has found something good toward him in this boy.
The LORD will raise up a king over Israel for himself who will cut off Jeroboam's family. That day is here. It's already beginning.

The LORD will strike Israel so it shakes like a reed in water. He'll pull Israel up by the roots from this good land he gave their ancestors and scatter them beyond the Euphrates, because they made Asherah poles and provoked the LORD to anger.
He'll give Israel up because of the sins Jeroboam committed and led Israel into.”
Jeroboam's wife got up and left for Tirzah. As she reached the threshold of her house, the boy died.
All Israel buried him and mourned for him, just as the LORD had said through his servant Ahijah the prophet.
The rest of Jeroboam's acts, his wars and how he ruled, are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jeroboam ruled for twenty-two years. Then he died and joined his ancestors, and his son Nadab became king in his place.

Solomon's son Rehoboam ruled in Judah. He was forty-one years old when he became king and ruled for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD had chosen from all the tribes of Israel for his name. His mother was Naamah from Ammon.
Judah did what was evil in the LORD's sight. Their sins stirred up his jealousy more than all their ancestors' sins had.
They built high places, sacred pillars, and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every leafy tree.
There were also male shrine prostitutes in the land. The people practiced the same detestable things as the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of Israel.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam's reign, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem.
He carried away the treasures of the LORD's house and the royal palace. He took everything, including all the gold shields Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them. He put them in the care of the guard commanders who watched the entrance to the palace.
Whenever the king went to the LORD's house, the guards carried the shields and then brought them back to the guardroom.
The rest of Rehoboam's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Rehoboam and Jeroboam were continually at war.
Rehoboam died and joined his ancestors and was buried with them in David's City. His mother was Naamah from Ammon. His son Abijam became king in his place.
In the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijam became king of Judah.
He ruled in Jerusalem for three years. His mother was Maacah daughter of Abishalom.
He followed all the sinful ways of his father before him. His heart wasn't fully devoted to the LORD his God as the heart of his ancestor David had been.
Still, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem by raising up his son to succeed him and keeping Jerusalem secure.
David had done what was right in the LORD's eyes and had followed everything the LORD commanded all his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
Rehoboam and Jeroboam were at war all through Rehoboam's life.
The rest of Abijam's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. Abijam and Jeroboam were at war.
Abijam died and joined his ancestors. They buried him in David's City, and his son Asa became king in his place.
In the twentieth year of King Jeroboam's reign over Israel, Asa became king of Judah.
He ruled in Jerusalem for forty-one years. His mother was Maacah daughter of Abishalom.
Asa did what was right in the LORD's eyes, as his ancestor David had done.
He drove the male shrine prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols his ancestors had made.
He removed his mother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah. Asa cut it down and burned it by the Kidron stream.
The high places remained, though Asa was fully devoted to the LORD all his life.
He brought the silver, gold, and utensils that he and his father had dedicated into the LORD's house.
Asa and King Baasha of Israel were at war throughout their reigns.
King Baasha of Israel moved against Judah and fortified Ramah to block anyone from coming or going from the territory of Asa king of Judah.

Asa took all the silver and gold left in the treasuries of the LORD's house and the palace and handed it to his servants. King Asa sent them to Ben Hadad son of Tabrimmon and grandson of Hezion, the king of Syria, who lived in Damascus. He sent this message:
“Let's make a treaty like the one our fathers made. I'm sending you silver and gold as a gift. Break your treaty with King Baasha of Israel so he'll withdraw from my land.”
Ben Hadad listened to King Asa and sent his army commanders against Israel's towns. They struck Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maacah, all Chinneroth, and the whole land of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard what had happened, he stopped building Ramah and stayed in Tirzah.
King Asa issued an order to all Judah, with no exceptions. They carried away the stone and timber Baasha had used to build Ramah. King Asa used it to build up Geba in Benjamin and Mizpah.
The rest of Asa's acts, his strength, all he did, and the towns he built are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. In his old age he developed a disease in his feet.
Asa died and joined his ancestors. He was buried with them in the city of his ancestor David, and his son Jehoshaphat became king in his place.
Jeroboam's son Nadab became king of Israel in the second year of King Asa's reign over Judah, and he ruled Israel for two years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, following his father's ways and repeating the sin his father had led Israel into.
Baasha son of Ahijah, from the tribe of Issachar, plotted against Nadab. As Nadab and all Israel were besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon, Baasha struck him down there.
Baasha killed Nadab in the third year of King Asa's reign over Judah and became king in Nadab's place.
As soon as Baasha became king, he struck down Jeroboam's entire family. He left no one in the family alive, just as the LORD had said through his servant Ahijah from Shiloh.
This happened because Jeroboam had sinned and led Israel into sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger.
The rest of Nadab's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Asa and King Baasha of Israel were at war throughout their reigns.
In the third year of King Asa's reign over Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king over all Israel. He ruled in Tirzah for twenty-four years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He followed Jeroboam's ways and repeated the sin Jeroboam had led Israel into.
The LORD gave Jehu son of Hanani this message against Baasha:
“I raised you from the dust and made you ruler over my people Israel. But you've followed Jeroboam's ways and led my people Israel into sin, provoking me to anger with their sins.
So I'll sweep away Baasha and his family completely. I'll make your household like the household of Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Dogs will eat Baasha's descendants who die in the city, and birds will eat those who die in the fields.”
The rest of Baasha's acts, what he did, and the power he showed are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Baasha died and joined his ancestors and was buried in Tirzah. His son Elah became king in his place.

The LORD's message came through Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha and his family because of all the evil Baasha did in the LORD's sight. He provoked the LORD with what he did, behaving like Jeroboam's family, and he had struck down that family too.
In the twenty-sixth year of King Asa's reign over Judah, Baasha's son Elah became king of Israel. He ruled in Tirzah for two years.
Elah's servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, plotted against him. Elah was in Tirzah getting drunk at the home of Arza, who managed the palace household there.
Zimri went in and struck Elah down, killing him in the twenty-seventh year of King Asa's reign over Judah. Zimri became king in his place.
As soon as he took the throne, Zimri attacked Baasha's whole household. He left no male alive, whether a relative or a friend.
Zimri wiped out Baasha's entire family, just as the LORD had said through the prophet Jehu.
This happened because Baasha and his son Elah had sinned and led Israel into sin. They provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols.
The rest of Elah's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
In the twenty-seventh year of King Asa's reign over Judah, Zimri ruled for seven days in Tirzah. At the time the Israelite army was camped near Gibbethon, a Philistine town.
The troops in camp heard that Zimri had plotted against the king and killed him. That very day, all Israel there in the camp made Omri, the army commander, king of Israel.
Omri and all Israel went up from Gibbethon and besieged Tirzah.
When Zimri saw that the city had been taken, he went into the fortified part of the royal palace, set the palace on fire over himself, and died.
He died for the sins he'd committed, doing what was evil in the LORD's eyes, following Jeroboam's ways, and repeating the sin Jeroboam had led Israel into.
The rest of Zimri's acts and the treason he committed are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Then the people of Israel split in two. Half followed Tibni son of Ginath and wanted to make him king. The other half followed Omri.
Omri's supporters overpowered the supporters of Tibni son of Ginath. Tibni died, and Omri became king.
In the thirty-first year of King Asa's reign over Judah, Omri became king of Israel. He ruled for twelve years, six of them in Tirzah.
Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver. He built a city on the hill and called it Samaria after Shemer, who had owned the hill.
Omri did what was evil in the LORD's sight and acted more wickedly than all those who came before him.
He followed all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, repeating the sins Jeroboam had led Israel into and provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, with worthless idols.
The rest of Omri's acts and the power he showed are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Omri died and joined his ancestors. He was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab became king in his place.
In the thirty-eighth year of King Asa's reign over Judah, Omri's son Ahab became king of Israel. He ruled Israel from Samaria for twenty-two years.
Ahab son of Omri did more evil in the LORD's eyes than anyone who came before him.
As if following the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat were a small thing, Ahab married Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and went to serve and worship Baal.
He put up an altar for Baal in the temple he had built for Baal in Samaria.
Ahab also made an Asherah pole. He provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger more than any king of Israel before him.

During Ahab's reign, Hiel from Bethel rebuilt Jericho. Laying the foundation cost him his firstborn son Abiram, and setting up the gates cost him his youngest son Segub. This was just as the LORD had said through Joshua son of Nun.
Elijah the Tishbite, one of the settlers of Gilead, told Ahab, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel I serve, lives, there will be no dew or rain in the coming years until I give the word.”
Then the LORD gave Elijah this message:
“Leave here, go east, and hide beside the Cherith stream near the Jordan.
You'll drink from the stream. I've ordered the ravens to feed you there.”
Elijah did what the LORD told him. He went and lived beside the Cherith stream near the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and again in the evening, and he drank from the stream.
After a while the stream dried up because no rain had fallen in the land.
Then the LORD gave him another message:
“Get up, go to Zarephath in Sidon, and stay there. I've commanded a widow there to provide for you.”
So Elijah went to Zarephath. When he reached the city gate, he found a widow gathering sticks. He called to her, “Please bring me a little water to drink in a jar.”
As she went to get it, he called after her, “Please bring me a bite of bread too.”

She replied, “As surely as the LORD your God lives, I have nothing baked. There's just a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in another jar. I'm gathering a couple of sticks so I can go home and make one last meal for my son and me. Then we'll eat it and die.”
Elijah said to her, “Don't be afraid. Go ahead and do what you said. Just make me a small loaf first and bring it out to me. Then make some for yourself and your son.
Because this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘The flour in the jar won't run out, and the oil in the jar won't run dry until the day the LORD sends rain on the land.’”
She went and did what Elijah said. She, Elijah, and her household had food for many days.
The flour never ran out, and the oil never ran dry, just as the LORD had promised through Elijah.
Later, the son of the woman who owned the house got sick. He grew so ill that he stopped breathing.
The woman said to Elijah, “What do you have against me, man of God? Did you come here to bring up my sin and kill my son?”
“Give me your son,” Elijah said. He took him from her arms, carried him upstairs to the room where he was staying, and laid him on his bed.
He cried out to the LORD, “LORD my God, have you brought disaster even on the widow I'm staying with by taking her son's life?”
