He stretched himself over the child three times and cried out to the LORD, “LORD my God, please let this child's life come back into him.”
The LORD listened to Elijah. The child's life returned, and he came back to life.
Elijah carried the child downstairs from his room and gave him back to his mother. “Look,” he said, “your son is alive.”
The woman told Elijah, “Now I know you're a man of God and that the LORD's word you speak is true.”
After a long time, in the third year, the LORD told Elijah, “Go present yourself to Ahab, and I'll send rain on the land.”
So Elijah went to see Ahab. By then the famine in Samaria was severe.
Ahab summoned Obadiah, who managed his household. Obadiah had great reverence for the LORD.
When Jezebel was killing the LORD's prophets, Obadiah had taken a hundred of them and hidden them in two caves, fifty in each. He supplied them with bread and water.
Ahab told Obadiah, “Go through the land and check every spring and stream. Maybe we'll find enough grass to keep the horses and mules alive so we don't lose all our animals.”
They divided the land between them to search it. Ahab went one way on his own, and Obadiah went another way on his own.
As Obadiah was on the road, Elijah met him. Obadiah recognized him, fell facedown, and said, “Is it really you, my lord Elijah?”
“Yes, it's me,” Elijah said. “Go tell your master, ‘Elijah is here!’”
Obadiah replied, “What wrong have I done that you'd hand me over to Ahab to be killed?

As surely as the LORD your God lives, there's no nation or kingdom my master hasn't sent people to search for you. When they said, ‘He isn't here,’ he made the nation or kingdom swear they hadn't found you.
And now you're telling me to go to my master and say, ‘Elijah is here!’

As soon as I leave you, the LORD's Spirit could carry you somewhere I don't know. Then I'll tell Ahab, he'll come looking for you, and when he can't find you he'll kill me. I've honored the LORD since I was young.
Haven't you heard what I did when Jezebel was killing the LORD's prophets? I hid a hundred of them, fifty to a cave, and gave them bread and water.
Now you want me to tell my master, ‘Elijah is here.’ He'll kill me!”
Elijah answered, “As surely as the LORD of Armies, whom I serve, lives, I'll present myself to Ahab today.”
So Obadiah went to Ahab and told him. Then Ahab went to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw him, he asked, “Is that you, the one who's been making trouble for Israel?”
Elijah answered, “I haven't made trouble for Israel. You and your father's family did that when you abandoned the LORD's commands and went after the Baals.
Now send word and gather all Israel to meet me at Mount Carmel. Bring the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of Asherah who eat at Jezebel's table.”
So Ahab sent word throughout Israel and gathered the prophets on Mount Carmel.
Elijah stepped forward and asked the people, “How long will you keep going back and forth between two sides? If the LORD is God, follow him. If Baal is, follow him.” Nobody said a word.
Then Elijah told the people, “I'm the only prophet of the LORD left here, and Baal has four hundred and fifty prophets.
Bring us two bulls. Let them choose one, cut it up, and lay it on the wood without lighting a fire. I'll prepare the other bull and lay it on the wood without lighting a fire either.
Call on the name of your god, and I'll call on the name of the LORD. The God who answers with fire is God.” All the people said, “That's fair.”
Elijah told Baal's prophets, “Choose a bull and prepare yours first, since there are so many of you. Call on your god's name, but don't light the fire.”
They prepared the bull they'd been given and called on Baal from morning until noon. “Baal, answer us!” they shouted. There was no voice and nobody answered. They jumped around the altar they'd made.
At noon Elijah began mocking them. “Shout louder! He's a god, after all. Maybe he's lost in thought, stepped away, or gone on a trip. Maybe he's asleep and somebody needs to wake him.”
They shouted louder and cut themselves with knives and spears as their custom was, until blood poured out.
They kept prophesying past midday until the time of the evening offering. There was no voice, no answer, and nobody paid attention.
Then Elijah told everyone, “Come closer.” They gathered around him, and he repaired the LORD's altar, which had been torn down.
Elijah took twelve stones, one for each tribe descended from Jacob, the man the LORD had told, “Your name will be Israel.”
He built an altar with the stones in the LORD's name. He dug a trench around it large enough to hold two seahs of seed.
He arranged the wood, cut up the bull, and laid it on the wood. Then he said, “Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and the wood.”
“Do it again,” he said, and they did. “Do it a third time,” he said, and they did it a third time.
Water ran down around the altar, and the trench filled with water too.

At the time of the evening offering, Elijah the prophet stepped forward and prayed, “LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let everyone know today that you are God in Israel, I am your servant, and I've done all this at your word.
Answer me, LORD, answer me so these people will know that you are God and that you've turned their hearts back to you.”
The LORD's fire fell and burned up the offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust. It licked up the water in the trench.
When the people saw it, they fell facedown and cried, “The LORD is God! The LORD is God!”
Elijah told them, “Seize Baal's prophets! Don't let any escape!” They seized them, and Elijah took them down to the Kishon stream and killed them there.
Then Elijah told Ahab, “Go on up and eat and drink. I hear the sound of heavy rain.”
Ahab went up to eat and drink, while Elijah climbed to the top of Carmel, bent low to the ground, and put his face between his knees.
He told his servant, “Go up and look toward the sea.” The servant looked and said, “There's nothing.” Elijah kept telling him to go back, seven times in all.

The seventh time the servant reported, “A small cloud the size of a man's hand is coming up out of the sea.” Elijah told him, “Go tell Ahab, ‘Get your chariot ready and head down before the rain stops you.’”
Soon the sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and heavy rain poured down. Ahab rode toward Jezreel.
The LORD's hand was on Elijah. He tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab to the entrance to Jezreel.
Ahab told Jezebel everything Elijah had done, including how he'd killed all the prophets with the sword.
Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah: “May the gods punish me severely if by this time tomorrow I haven't made your life end like theirs!”
When Elijah saw what was happening, he ran for his life. When he reached Beersheba in Judah, he left his servant there.
Elijah went a day's journey into the wilderness alone and sat down under a juniper tree. He asked to die. “I've had enough, LORD,” he said. “Take my life. I'm no better than my ancestors.”
He lay down under the juniper tree and fell asleep. An angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat.”
He looked and saw a loaf baked on hot coals and a jar of water beside his head. He ate and drank, then lay down again.
The angel of the LORD came back, touched him, and said, “Get up and eat. The journey ahead is too much for you.”
Elijah got up, ate, and drank. That food gave him strength to travel forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God.
He found a cave there and stayed in it. The LORD spoke to him and asked, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

Elijah said, “I've been deeply devoted to the LORD, the God of Armies. But the Israelites have abandoned your covenant, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I'm the only one left, and now they're trying to kill me too.”

The LORD said, “Go outside and stand on the mountain before the LORD.” As the LORD passed by, a mighty wind tore through the mountains and shattered rocks before him. The LORD wasn't in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake, but the LORD wasn't in the earthquake.
After the earthquake came a fire, but the LORD wasn't in the fire. After the fire came a quiet, gentle voice.
When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his cloak and went out to stand at the mouth of the cave. A voice asked him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

Elijah said, “I've been deeply devoted to the LORD, the God of Armies. But the Israelites have abandoned your covenant, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I'm the only one left, and now they're trying to kill me too.”
The LORD told him, “Go back the way you came, to the wilderness of Damascus. When you get there, anoint Hazael as king over Syria.
Anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel, and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel Meholah to take your place as prophet.
Anyone who escapes Hazael's sword will be killed by Jehu, and anyone who escapes Jehu's sword will be killed by Elisha.
But I've kept seven thousand people in Israel, every one whose knees have never bowed to Baal and whose lips have never kissed him.”
Elijah left and found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing with twelve teams of oxen. Elisha was working the twelfth team. Elijah went over and put his cloak on him.
Elisha left his oxen and ran after Elijah. “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I'll follow you.” Elijah said, “Go back. What have I done to you?”
Elisha went back, killed his team of oxen, and used their equipment to cook the meat. He gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he got up, followed Elijah, and became his attendant.
King Ben Hadad of Syria gathered his whole army, along with thirty-two allied kings and their horses and chariots. He laid siege to Samaria and attacked it.
He sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel. They told him, “This is what Ben Hadad says:
‘Your silver and gold are mine, and so are the best of your wives and children.’”
The king of Israel answered, “As you say, my lord the king. I belong to you, and so does everything I have.”
The messengers came back and said, “Ben Hadad says, ‘I already demanded that you hand over your silver and gold, your wives, and your children.
Around this time tomorrow I'll send my servants to search your palace and your officials' houses. They'll take away everything you value.’”
Then the king of Israel called all the elders of the land. “See how this man is looking for trouble,” he said. “He demanded my wives, my children, my silver, and my gold, and I didn't turn him down.”
All the elders and the people told him, “Don't listen to him. Don't agree to this.”
So Ahab told Ben Hadad's messengers, “Tell my lord the king, ‘I'll do everything you first asked of your servant, but I can't do this.’” The messengers took the answer back to Ben Hadad.
Ben Hadad sent back this reply: “May the gods punish me severely if there's enough dust left in Samaria for each man following me to take a handful.”
The king of Israel answered, “Tell him, ‘A man putting on his armor shouldn't boast like a man taking it off.’”
When Ben Hadad heard the message, he and the other kings were drinking in their shelters. He told his men, “Get ready to attack!” So they took their positions against the city.
A prophet came to Ahab king of Israel and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘See this huge army? I'm handing it over to you today. Then you'll know that I am the LORD.’”
“Through whom?” Ahab asked. The prophet replied, “The LORD says, ‘Through the young men serving the provincial officials.’” Ahab asked, “Who should start the battle?” The prophet answered, “You.”
Ahab called up the young men who served the provincial officials. There were two hundred and thirty-two of them. Then he called up the rest of the Israelite troops, seven thousand in all.
They marched out at noon. By then Ben Hadad and the thirty-two kings helping him were getting drunk in their shelters.
The young men serving the provincial officials went out first. Ben Hadad sent scouts out, and they reported, “Men are coming out of Samaria.”
He said, “Whether they've come out for peace or for battle, take them alive.”
The young men serving the provincial officials came out of the city with the army behind them.
Each struck down the man he faced. The Syrians ran, and Israel chased them. King Ben Hadad of Syria escaped on horseback with some horsemen.
The king of Israel went out, struck the horses and chariots, and inflicted heavy losses on the Syrians.
Then the prophet came to the king of Israel and told him, “Go strengthen your forces and decide what you need to do. When the year comes around again, the king of Syria will attack you.”
The king of Syria's officials told him, “Their god is a god of the hills. That's why they were stronger than us. If we fight them on the plain, we'll surely be stronger than they are.
Here's what to do. Remove the kings from their commands and put officers in their places.
Raise an army like the one you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot. We'll fight them on the plain and surely overpower them.” The king listened and did what they said.
When the year came around again, Ben Hadad gathered the Syrian army and went up to Aphek to fight Israel.
The Israelites were called up, given supplies, and sent out to meet them. Israel camped opposite them like two little flocks of young goats, while the Syrians filled the land.

A man of God came to the king of Israel and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because the Syrians say the LORD is a god of the hills and has no power in the valleys, I'll hand this entire army over to you. Then you'll know that I am the LORD.’”
The two armies camped opposite each other for seven days. On the seventh day the battle began, and the Israelites struck down a hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in a single day.
The survivors ran into the city of Aphek, and its wall collapsed on twenty-seven thousand of them. Ben Hadad escaped into the city and hid in an inner room.
His officials told him, “We've heard that Israel's kings are merciful. Let us put sackcloth around our bodies and ropes on our heads and go out to the king of Israel. Maybe he'll let you live.”
They put on sackcloth and ropes and went to the king of Israel. “Your servant Ben Hadad says, ‘Please let me live,’” they said. Ahab replied, “Is he still alive? He's my brother.”

The men were watching for any sign of mercy and latched onto his words. “Your brother Ben Hadad,” they said. “Go bring him,” Ahab replied. When Ben Hadad came out to him, Ahab invited him up into his chariot.

Ben Hadad told him, “I'll give back the towns my father took from yours. You can set up trading streets in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria.” Ahab said, “I'll release you under that agreement.” So he made a treaty with him and let him go.
One of the members of the prophets' company told another at the LORD's command, “Please strike me.” The man refused.
The prophet told him, “Because you didn't obey the LORD's voice, a lion will kill you as soon as you leave me.” As soon as the man left, a lion found him and killed him.
The prophet found another man and said, “Please strike me.” The man struck him and wounded him.
The prophet then stood beside the road to wait for the king. He disguised himself by pulling his headband down over his eyes.

As the king passed by, the prophet called out to him: “I went into the middle of the battle, and someone brought me a prisoner. He told me, ‘Guard this man. If he gets away, you'll pay with your life or a talent of silver.’
While I was busy here and there, the prisoner slipped away.” The king of Israel answered, “That's your sentence, then. You've pronounced it yourself.”
The man quickly pulled the headband off his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.

He told the king, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You let the man I had set apart for destruction slip out of your hands. Your life will take the place of his life, and your people will take the place of his people.’”
The king of Israel went home to Samaria sullen and angry.
Some time after this, Naboth from Jezreel owned a vineyard in Jezreel beside the palace of Ahab, king of Samaria.
Ahab told Naboth, “Let me have your vineyard for a vegetable garden. It's right by my house. I'll give you a better vineyard in exchange, or I can pay you what it's worth if you prefer.”
Naboth replied, “May the LORD forbid me from giving you the land I inherited from my ancestors!”
Ahab went home sullen and angry because Naboth from Jezreel had told him, “I won't give you my ancestral land.” Ahab lay down on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat.
His wife Jezebel came in and asked, “Why are you so upset that you won't eat?”
He answered, “I offered to buy Naboth's vineyard or give him another one in exchange if he wanted it. He said, ‘I won't give you my vineyard.’”
His wife Jezebel said, “Aren't you the one who rules Israel? Get up, eat something, and cheer up. I'll get you Naboth's vineyard.”
She wrote letters in Ahab's name, sealed them with his seal, and sent them to the elders and nobles who lived in Naboth's city.
In the letters she said, “Call a fast and seat Naboth in a prominent place among the people.
Sit two scoundrels opposite him and have them accuse him of cursing God and the king. Then take him out and stone him to death.”
The elders and nobles of the city did exactly what Jezebel told them to do in the letters she sent.
They called a fast and gave Naboth a prominent seat among the people.
The two scoundrels came in and sat across from him. In front of everyone they testified, “Naboth cursed God and the king!” Then the people took him outside the city and stoned him to death.
They sent Jezebel word: “Naboth has been stoned to death.”
When Jezebel heard that Naboth was dead, she told Ahab, “Get up and take possession of the vineyard Naboth from Jezreel refused to sell you. He's dead.”
When Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he got up and went down to Naboth's vineyard to take possession of it.
Then the LORD gave this message to Elijah the Tishbite:
“Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who lives in Samaria. He's in Naboth's vineyard, where he's gone to take possession of it.

Tell him, ‘This is what the LORD says: “Have you murdered a man and taken his property too?”’ Then tell him, ‘This is what the LORD says: “Where the dogs licked up Naboth's blood, they'll lick up your blood too.”’”
Ahab asked Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” Elijah replied, “I found you because you've sold yourself to do what's evil in the LORD's sight.
He says, ‘I'll bring disaster on you and sweep you away completely. I'll cut off every male in Ahab's family in Israel, whether shut in or free.
I'll make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you've provoked me to anger and led Israel into sin.’”
The LORD also spoke about Jezebel: “Dogs will eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.
Dogs will eat anyone from Ahab's family who dies in the city, and birds will eat anyone who dies out in the fields.”
No one sold himself to do what was evil in the LORD's eyes like Ahab did, spurred on by his wife Jezebel.
He did detestable things by following idols, just as the Amorites had done before the LORD drove them out ahead of the Israelites.
When Ahab heard these words, he tore his clothes, dressed in sackcloth, and fasted. He slept in sackcloth and went around dejected.
Then the LORD gave Elijah the Tishbite this message:
“Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself, I won't bring disaster in his lifetime. I'll bring it on his family in his son's time.”
For three years there was no war between Syria and Israel.
In the third year King Jehoshaphat of Judah went down to visit the king of Israel.
The king of Israel asked his officials, “You know Ramoth Gilead belongs to us, don't you? Why are we sitting here instead of taking it back from the king of Syria?”
Then he asked Jehoshaphat, “Will you go with me to fight at Ramoth Gilead?” Jehoshaphat answered, “I'm with you. My people are your people, and my horses are your horses.”
But Jehoshaphat added, “Please ask what the LORD has to say first.”
So the king of Israel gathered about four hundred prophets and asked them, “Should I go to war against Ramoth Gilead or hold back?” They said, “Go. The Lord will hand it over to the king.”
Jehoshaphat asked, “Isn't there another prophet of the LORD here we can ask?”

The king of Israel answered, “There's still one man we can ask for the LORD's word, Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him. He never prophesies anything good about me, only disaster.” Jehoshaphat said, “The king shouldn't talk like that.”
Then the king of Israel called an officer and said, “Get Micaiah son of Imlah here quickly.”
The king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah were sitting on their thrones in royal robes in an open area at the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were prophesying before them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made himself iron horns. He said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘With these you'll drive back the Syrians until they're destroyed.’”
All the other prophets gave the same message: “Go up to Ramoth Gilead and win! The LORD will hand it over to the king.”
The messenger who went to get Micaiah told him, “All the prophets are telling the king the same good news. Please agree with them and give him good news too.”
Micaiah replied, “As surely as the LORD lives, I'll say only what the LORD tells me.”
When Micaiah came in, the king asked him, “Should we go to war at Ramoth Gilead or hold back?” Micaiah answered, “Go and win! The LORD will hand it over to the king.”
The king said, “How many times do I have to make you swear to tell me only the truth in the LORD's name?”
Micaiah answered, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. The LORD said, ‘These people have no master. Let each one go home in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Didn't I tell you? He never prophesies good for me, only disaster.”
Micaiah said, “Then hear the LORD's word. I saw the LORD sitting on his throne with the whole army of heaven standing on his right and his left.
The LORD asked, ‘Who will lure Ahab into going up to Ramoth Gilead so he falls there?’ One suggested one thing and another suggested something else.
Then a spirit stepped forward, stood before the LORD, and said, ‘I'll lure him.’
‘How?’ the LORD asked. The spirit said, ‘I'll go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ The LORD said, ‘You'll lure him and succeed. Go do it.’
So the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours. The LORD has declared disaster for you.”
Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah went up and slapped Micaiah across the cheek. “Which way did the LORD's Spirit go when he left me to speak to you?” he asked.
Micaiah answered, “You'll find out the day you go into an inner room to hide.”
The king of Israel ordered, “Take Micaiah back to Amon the city governor and Joash the king's son.
Tell them the king says, ‘Put this man in prison. Give him only bread and water to keep him alive until I return safely.’”
Micaiah answered, “If you come back safely, the LORD hasn't spoken through me.” Then he called out, “Listen to this, all of you!”
So the king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah went to Ramoth Gilead.
The king of Israel told Jehoshaphat, “I'll go into battle in disguise, but you wear your royal robes.” So he disguised himself and went into battle.
Meanwhile the king of Syria had ordered his thirty-two chariot commanders, “Don't fight anyone, great or small, except the king of Israel.”
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they thought, “That must be the king of Israel!” They turned toward him to fight, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
When they realized he wasn't the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him.
But a man shot an arrow at random and hit the king of Israel between the joints of his armor. The king told his chariot driver, “Turn around and get me out of the battle. I'm badly wounded.”
The fighting grew fiercer that day. The king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, and he died that evening. Blood from his wound had run into the bottom of the chariot.
Around sunset a shout went through the army: “Everyone back to your town! Everyone back to your own land!”
The king died, and they took him back to Samaria and buried him there.
They washed his chariot at the pool of Samaria, where the prostitutes bathed, and the dogs licked up his blood, just as the LORD had said.
The rest of Ahab's acts, everything he did, the ivory palace he built, and all the towns he built are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Ahab died and joined his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king in his place.
Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah in the fourth year of King Ahab's reign over Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five when he became king, and he ruled for twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Azubah daughter of Shilhi.
He followed the ways of his father Asa and didn't turn away from them. He did what was right in the LORD's eyes. But the high places remained, and people still sacrificed and burned incense there.
Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel.
The rest of Jehoshaphat's acts, the power he showed, and his wars are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
He drove out the male shrine prostitutes who had remained in the land after the reign of his father Asa.
There was no king in Edom at that time. A deputy ruled there.
Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to sail to Ophir for gold. They never went because they were wrecked at Ezion Geber.
Ahaziah son of Ahab told Jehoshaphat, “Let my men sail with yours.” Jehoshaphat refused.
Jehoshaphat died and joined his ancestors. He was buried with them in the city of his ancestor David, and his son Jehoram became king in his place.
Ahab's son Ahaziah became king over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of King Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah. He ruled Israel for two years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He followed the ways of his father and mother and of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into sin.
He served and worshiped Baal and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done in every way.
